newsitem.title: HUNGARY: HUNGARIAN COMPANIES SEE SALES RISE IN 1997 - SURVEY.
newsitem.headline: HUNGARIAN COMPANIES SEE SALES RISE IN 1997 - SURVEY.

text.p: Most Hungarian enterprises expect sales to rise in 1996 but believe growth is hampered by weak domestic demand, a survey published on Thursday showed.

The survey, conducted jointly by GKI Economic Research and two employer organisations, said the 767 companies sampled for the survey expect total sales in 1997 to rise by 3.1 percent on weighted average over 1996 levels.
Some 31 percent of the contributing companies forecast improving profitability for 1997, while only 21 percent expected a downturn, survey officials told a news conference.

But despite expectations of growth, the companies generally lack confidence in the government, are worried about unfair competition and do not expect the economy to improve all that much, the officials added.
"The companies painted a more pessimistic picture about the general situtation -- no better than last September," said GKI Economic Research General Director Andras Vertes.

The survey found that 55 percent contributors saw weak domestic demand as a major obstacle to growth, up from 48 percent in a 1995 survey, while the unpredictability of politics was cited by 41 percent, up from 33 percent.

"The situation of lost confidence (in the government and the market) is very dangerous," said Istvan Orban, president of the Hungarian Employers' Alliance, a sponsor of the survey. "This could make entrepreneurs blame others for their own mistakes."

Tamas Bihall, chairman of the Hungarian Commercial and Industrial Chamber, added that low demand in Hungary could weaken the country's chances for European Union membership, expected sometime after the year 2000.
"During our (future) membership talks with the European Union, low domestic demand may create a rather bad position for the country," he said.
The publishers said it was a good sign for the economy that the companies expected investments to grow by seven percent in 1997, compared with an estimate of up to two percent in 1996.

But they added that the modernisation of the economy would demand double-digit investment growth, and 20 percent of the companies planning investments wanted to buy new technologies, while 60 percent only wanted to replace depreciated equipment.
